knowledge_point.title: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{1}{|9 x|\sqrt{(9 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=9 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=9,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{9})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

The substitution factor is positive, so the absolute values satisfy

$$
|u|=|9 x|=9|x|,\qquad \frac{1}{|x|}=\frac{9}{|u|}.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|9 x|\sqrt{(9 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 1\int \frac{1}{|9 x|\sqrt{(9 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 1(\frac{1}{9})\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}}{9}+C \\  &= \frac{\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(9 x \right)}}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This antiderivative applies on either interval where $|9 x|>1$; the constant may differ between those intervals.
